Gaps / UNVERIFIED (search budget exhausted) - 2016 white paper U-turn dates; the 2022 white paper "all schools in strong trusts by 2030" and the withdrawn Schools Bill. - MAT share of academies; IFS work on MATs; a Bertoni–Gibbons–Silva MAT paper. - National-curriculum commencement for academies (Sept 2026 or 2028). - Décret Hamon number; REP+ coefficient 1.1; NOTRe transport date; share of schools on 4 days. - How France derives 720 h at secondary in EAG. - The OECD TALIS 2024 full-time average (~41 h) comes from press reports only. --- Summary: 10 most useful facts for a French note on ORS and autonomy 1. England has no teaching-hours maximum . The STPCD sets 195 days and 1,265 h of directed time at the head's disposal, plus ≥10% PPA (STPCD 2026, §52.2, 52.5, 53.4). France fixes 18 h (certifiés) / 15 h (agrégés) / 24 h + 108 h (PE) per week nationally. 2. OECD 2025: France's statutory teaching time is 900 / 720 / 720 h (primary / lower / upper secondary) against an OECD average of 770 / 710 / 678 . England reports none; its actual teaching time is 893 / 777 / 777 h over 190 days (France 162 days in primary). 3. Real workload: English full-time teachers report 50.1 h/week (2025, WLTL) and French full-time collège teachers 38.7 h (TALIS 2024). England did not take part in TALIS 2024. 4. TALIS 2018: England full-time lower secondary taught 20.5 h, close to the OECD average of about 21.5. The gap was 32.7 h of non-teaching tasks against about 26 h OECD . Teaching hours are not the difference; out-of-class load is. 5. 60.4% of English pupils (84% at secondary, 50% at primary) attend academies (Jan 2026). They are funded directly by DfE under a contract, outside LA control. 6. Autonomy has been partly re-centralised by the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026: a pay floor (2027), the national curriculum, QTS (2027), LA admissions powers, and the end of automatic academisation and of the free-school presumption. 7. Freedoms were little used for time : only 8% of academies lengthened the day and 4% changed terms (DfE 2014). Most trusts still follow the national pay scales (about 94%). 8. Causal evidence: autonomy worked for failing schools that gained the most autonomy plus a new head (+0.2 SD, Eyles & Machin, JEEA 2019). It had no effect for primary converters (Eyles, Machin & McNally 2017), and differences between MATs exceed the gap between academies and LA schools. 9. France's 4-day week covers 93% of communes (2023), despite the Cour des comptes (May 2025) judging it out of step with pupils' needs. The only causal study of the 2013 reform concerns mothers' employment (gender gap on Wednesday −15%, IPP 2017), not learning. 10. England pairs autonomy with strong outcome accountability : Progress 8 value-added, published tables, KS2 SATs (62% at the expected standard in 2025), now MAT-level tables, and Ofsted inspection of trusts from 2027-28. France has neither school-level value-added publication nor head control of service time.

titre: 02 — Groupes de niveau, groupes de besoins, tutorat : what the evidence says
texte: Research file for the note on school organisation. Compiled 2026-10-26. English, French quotes kept. Convention: UNVERIFIED = not checked against a primary or reliable secondary source in this session. "SD" = standard deviation; "months" = EEF months of additional progress. Caveat: the web-search budget ran out before the peer-effects and Slavin/Betts checks were done, so those items are marked. --- Bottom line on the claim being tested Claim: "There is no solid RCT evidence that ability grouping is ineffective, and the unions opposed the 2024 groupes de besoins citing research." Part of claim Verdict Why --- --- --- No solid RCT evidence that grouping is ineffective Largely true for between-class grouping; but there is no solid RCT evidence that it is effective in rich countries either. The best rich-country RCT (EEF/UCL "Best Practice in Setting", 127 schools) found ~0 effect, but fidelity collapsed, so it tests nothing cleanly. The one large clean RCT of tracking (Kenya, Duflo-Dupas-Kremer 2011) found +0.14 SD, including for low achievers . Meta-analyses of mostly non-experimental studies find between-class grouping ≈ 0 (g = 0.04 to 0.06). "Research shows grouping hurts weak pupils" (union line) Overstated. EEF reads a small negative for low attainers, on evidence it rates weak; Steenbergen-Hu et al. (2016) find effects "did not differ" by ability level; Kenya RCT finds gains for low achievers. Harm to the weakest is plausible when low groups get lower expectations and a thinner curriculum — the French IGÉSR observed exactly that in 2024-25. Unions cited research True. SNES-FSU (April 2024) cited Cnesco (Lafontaine 2017), Dupriez and Draelants (2004), Draelants (2023 interview). But the Cnesco text they quote also says homogeneous groups "peuvent permettre d'améliorer les résultats des élèves en difficulté" under conditions. The courts ruled on evidence False. Both Conseil d'État decisions turned on competence (who signs the text) and, in 2026, a minimal "erreur manifeste d'appréciation" review. No ruling on effectiveness. Strongest evidence in the area Tutoring and within-class / flexible regrouping , not permanent between-class setting. Nickow et al. (2020): 0.37 SD pooled over 96 RCTs; within-class grouping g = 0.19 to 0.30. --- A. France 2023-2026: what happened Timeline Date Act Content Source --- --- --- --- Dec 2023 Attal, « choc des savoirs » Announced "groupes de niveau" in français-maths, 6e-5e from 2024, 4e-3e from 2025. Renamed "groupes de besoins" in the final text. Context; naming change widely reported (UNVERIFIED exact date of the renaming) 15 Mar 2024 Arrêté (ministre) French and maths "organisés en groupes", formed "en fonction des besoins des élèves identifiés par les professeurs"; groups of the weakest pupils with reduced numbers; 6e-5e from 2024, 4e-3e from 2025. Conseil d'État, communiqué 28 Nov 2024, https://conseil-etat.fr/actualites/la-poursuite-des-groupes-de-besoins-au-college-a-la-rentree-2025-necessite-un-decret-du-premier-ministre 3 Apr 2024 SNES-FSU note « La recherche ne valide pas les groupes de niveau » See research cited below. https://www.aix.snes.edu/IMG/pdf/la recherche ne valide pas les groupes de niveau.pdf (PDF metadata date) 28 Nov 2024 CE, nos 493513 et al. (8 joined cases, unions and teachers) Annulled the group provisions: organisation of collège teaching belongs to the Prime Minister by décret , not a ministerial arrêté. Rejected the claim that groups are contrary to the collège unique (art. L.332-3 Code de l'éducation): curricula, hours and socle unchanged, about two-thirds of hours stay in the reference class, pupils can move groups. Annulment deferred to rentrée 2025. Same CE communiqué 4 Apr 2025 Décret + arrêté Décret allows an arrêté to create groups distinct from classes in 6e-5e. Arrêté re-creates groupes de besoins in 6e-5e; pupils may be regrouped in their reference class "dans la limite de dix semaines par an". 4e-3e dropped ; replaced by up to 2 h/week of support. Weka, https://www.weka.fr/actualite/education/article/les-groupes-de-besoins-au-college-sont-confirmes-pour-les-classes-de-6e-et-de-5e-198775/ ; Banque des Territoires, https://www.banquedesterritoires.fr/les-groupes-de-besoins-enterines-mais-limites-aux-classes-de-sixieme-et-cinquieme May 2025 (public 17 Jun 2025) IGÉSR report n° 24-25 007 (intermediate) See findings below. https://www.education.gouv.fr/igesr/mise-en-place-des-groupes-de-besoins-en-francais-et-mathematiques-465624 (page returned 403; findings via Banque des Territoires) 27 Feb 2026 CE, SNES, n° 506767 et s. Rejected the challenge to the 2025 décret/arrêté: décret may delegate to arrêté; choice "n'est pas entaché d'erreur manifeste d'appréciation", even though "comme le relève un rapport de l'IGÉSR de mai 2025" implementation is difficult. CE, https://conseil-etat.fr/actualites/le-conseil-d-etat-rejette-des-recours-contre-les-groupes-de-besoins-mis-en-place-au-college ; Landot, https://blog.landot-avocats.net/2026/03/01/colleges-apres-un-redoublement-le-decret-groupes-de-niveau-obtient-enfin-en-droit-une-bonne-note/ 10 Mar 2026 (JO 12 Mar) Arrêté amending arrêté of 19 May 2015 (JORFTEXT000053652601) Art. 3 repeals art. 4-1 (mandatory groups). Replaced from rentrée 2026 by an "accompagnement pédagogique renforcé" in 6e-5e: schools may form reduced-size groups and/or needs-based groups; up to 1 extra hour of support/enrichment in 6e for identified pupils. Banque des Territoires, https://www.banquedesterritoires.fr/au-college-les-groupes-de-besoins-sont-remplaces-par-un-accompagnement-pedagogique-renforce Status 2026-27 : groups are optional ; the government won in court and then dropped the obligation for policy reasons. (Minister's name at the time of the March 2026 arrêté: UNVERIFIED.) IGÉSR interim report (May 2025): what it found Sample: 39 collèges, 8 académies (some press: 9), year 2024-25. A wider 1,500-collège evaluation was announced for autumn 2025: result not found (UNVERIFIED whether published) . Source: https://www.banquedesterritoires.fr/groupes-de-besoins-au-college-un-premier-bilan-negatif - Most colleges formed level groups ; some formed mixed groups with smaller numbers; only "une infime minorité" formed groups around specific skills. - "une quasi-absence de mobilité" between groups; the 10-week return to the reference class was rarely used. - Pupils with high needs: the measure "n'a clairement pas bénéficié" to them; "risque majeur" of widening gaps before the return to full classes in 4e. - Groups made up mostly of pupils with low needs benefited most. - Teachers mostly responded to difficulty by lowering expectations and cutting content . - Recommendations: abandon the uniform model (all 6e-5e, full French-maths timetable), more autonomy for heads, train teachers in managing heterogeneity and severe difficulty. - Not a causal evaluation : no control group. No DEPP impact evaluation found (UNVERIFIED that none exists). Reading : the IGÉSR describes the textbook failure mode of the literature (fixed groups, low expectations in low groups, no regrouping), not a test of well-run flexible grouping. What the unions cited (SNES-FSU, April 2024) Cited Claim as used Comment --- --- --- Cnesco, consensus conference on differentiation (Cnesco and Ifé, March 2017) Within-class level groups can harm motivation; "ne doivent pas être installés dans le temps". Same dossier: homogeneous groups "au sein de la classe ou entre plusieurs classes peut permettre d'améliorer les résultats des élèves en difficulté", if tied to a precise objective, based on prior assessment, limited in time. Lafontaine (note Cnesco, 2017) Level classes help strong classes, hurt weak ones, widen gaps. Mostly cross-country/correlational (PISA-type). Not RCT. Dupriez and Draelants (2004, UCLouvain) Temporary flexible groups inside mixed classes can help all. Supports flexible grouping. Draelants, Café pédagogique (10 Oct 2023) Losses for weak pupils exceed gains for strong; teachers lower goals in weak groups. Interview, not a study. CNESCO 2015-16 mixité sociale work and Duru-Bellat / Monseur-Crahay: not cited in this SNES note; likely in other union material (UNVERIFIED). Cnesco's own sheet (Fiche thématique Différenciation, republished April 2025, https://www.cnesco.fr/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Fiche-thematique Differenciation-pedagogique Cnesco.pdf) recommends: "Regrouper temporairement des élèves autour d'un même besoin : le groupement doit être flexible et réévalué"; "prévoir la mise en place d'emplois du temps avec des heures en barrettes "; "Favoriser les classes hétérogènes, tout en organisant des groupes restreints temporaires". Context figures (TALIS 2013): 22% of French collège teachers report differentiated teaching vs 44% average; 37% have co-taught at least once vs 58%. France 1967-1983 "groupes de niveau-matière" No evaluation found. Only an APMEP practitioner article (Dec 1982) describing ten years of maths level groups at collège Dufy (Nice) and their "graves inconvénients", and a reference to the Legrand report (1983). https://bibnum.publimath.fr/AAA/AAA82035.pdf (content UNVERIFIED, search results only). Treat as no French causal evidence . --- B. Evidence on ability grouping, by design (i) Between-class grouping (tracking, streaming, setting) Source Design Result Notes / URL --- --- --- --- EEF Toolkit, setting/streaming (UK) Meta-synthesis (58 studies, review last updated July 2021) 0 months on average; −3 months for low attainers, +1 for high attainers; "not an effective way to raise attainment for most pupils"; evidence "very limited" (most studies old, few RCTs). The older −1 month figure (Tes, 2018) is superseded. Read directly 18 Nov 2026 (Chrome): https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/setting-and-streaming . VERIFIED. EEF content as reproduced by QRF / Evidence for Learning Same synthesis, other version 0 months , "very limited" evidence, 58 studies , many not RCTs; small negative for low attainers, small positive for high. https://qrf.org/index%2ephp/en/teaching-and-learning-toolkit/setting-and-streaming ; https://evidenceforlearning.org.au/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/setting-and-streaming . The −1 vs 0 gap is version difference, unexplained. Steenbergen-Hu, Makel and Olszewski-Kubilius (2016) , Review of Educational Research 86, 849-899 Second-order meta-analysis: 13 meta-analyses, 172 primary studies Between-class grouping g = 0.04 to 0.06 (≈ nil); within-class 0.19 to 0.30 ; cross-grade subject grouping 0.26 ; special grouping for gifted 0.37 . "Did not differ" for high, medium and low ability students. Abstract via https://www.accelerationinstitute.org/Research/Bibliography/Bibliography.aspx?ID=5 . A 2024 follow-up reportedly finds larger between-class effects: UNVERIFIED . Slavin (1987) , RER 57, 293-336 (elementary); Slavin (1990) , RER 60, 471-499 (secondary) Best-evidence syntheses 1990: no positive evidence for between-class grouping in secondary (Allan 1991 summary). 1987: regrouping for reading/maths across classes (Joplin-type) positive, whole-day ability classes not. Effect sizes UNVERIFIED (paywalled). Gutiérrez and Slavin (1992), Joplin-like nongraded reading programmes: median +0.46 , https://www.ascd.org/el/articles/response---the-nongraded-elementary-schoolgreat-potential-but-keep-it-simple Hattie (2009) Synthesis of meta-analyses Ability grouping d = 0.12 ; within-class grouping 0.16 (Table 6.1, p. 74), Lou et al. (1996) 0.17; gifted grouping ~0.30. Secondary sources only (https://aabner.org/ojs/index.php/bildungsforschung/article/download/205/301). Hattie's averaging is widely criticised. EEF/UCL "Best Practice in Grouping Students" (Francis et al.), Intervention A: Best Practice in Setting Cluster RCT, 127 schools , Years 7-8, 2 years Maths ES = −0.01 , English ES = −0.08 : "no evidence that the intervention improves outcomes". Half of maths schools and over half of English schools stopped before follow-up ; buy-in "low"; high test attrition. Intervention B (mixed attainment): feasibility pilot only, no impact estimate. https://ncm.gu.se/2018/09/grouping-students-by-achievement . Reading : tests "better setting vs usual setting", not "setting vs mixed"; uninformative on the core question. UCL later used a matched non-random design because grouping changes "take time and effort". Betts (2011) , Handbook of the Economics of Education vol. 3, ch. 7 Review Conclusions UNVERIFIED (paywalled). https://ideas.repec.org/h/eee/educhp/3-07.html Collins and Gan (2013) , NBER WP 18848, Dallas IV, ~9,000 pupils, 135 schools, grades 3-4 Homogeneous sorting by prior score raises maths and reading across the distribution , high and low. Magnitudes in summaries (0.4 SD; 1.6× for high achievers): UNVERIFIED . https://www.nber.org/papers/w18848 . NEPC review: tracking inferred from score distributions, "too weak" for policy. Card and Giuliano (2016) , AER 106(10), 2783-2816 RD + between-cohort, US urban district, grade 4 High-achiever classes: Black and Hispanic participants +0.5 SD reading and maths, persisting to grade 6; no spillovers on non-participants ; peers/teacher quality explain ~10%. https://www.nber.org/papers/w22104 . High end of the distribution only. Cortes, Goodman and Nomi (2015) , JHR, Chicago "double-dose algebra" RD, 9th graders below national median Double period of algebra (with more homogeneous classes): ACT maths +0.15 SD , college enrolment +8.6 pp (mostly 2-year); no short-run gain in algebra failure. https://www.nber.org/papers/w20211.pdf . Bundles extra time with grouping; best low-achiever evidence in rich country. (ii) Within-class grouping - EEF Toolkit, within-class attainment grouping : about +3 months , evidence rating cut from "moderate" to "limited"; "likely to be beneficial for all learners", "less benefit for lower attaining pupils". Older/other versions: +2 months , "very limited", 22 studies . https://www.tes.com/news/exclusive-mixed-ability-classes-more-effective-sets ; https://evidenceforlearning.org.au/toolkit/within-class-achievement-grouping - Steenbergen-Hu et al. (2016): g = 0.19 to 0.30 . Lou et al. (1996): +0.17 vs no grouping; homogeneous vs heterogeneous small groups +0.12 (via Hattie summaries). (iii) RCTs and quasi-RCTs of regrouping by level Study Design Result --- --- --- Duflo, Dupas and Kremer (2011) , AER 101(5), 1739-1774 RCT , 121 Kenyan schools (61 random assignment vs 60 tracking), grade 1 Tracking schools +0.14 SD after 18 months, persisting one year after . "Students at all levels of the distribution benefited"; pupils near the median gained similarly in upper or lower section. Positive direct peer effect, but tracking let teachers "teach to their level". https://www.nber.org/papers/w14475 . Context: classes split thanks to an extra (contract) teacher programme, so both arms had smaller classes (details UNVERIFIED this session). Teaching at the Right Level (Banerjee et al. 2016, NBER WP 22746; JEP 2017 31(4), 73-102) Series of RCTs, India Regroup pupils by actual level (not grade) for part of the day. Haryana (teachers, dedicated hour): language +0.15 SD . Uttar Pradesh (volunteer "learning camps", 40 days + 10-day summer camps, during school hours): +0.70 SD . Training/materials alone: no effect. https://www.nber.org/papers/w22746 ; https://www.aeaweb.org/research/proof-of-concept-scalable-policy-rct-challenges TaRL Zambia "Catch Up" (de Barros and Lubozha, J-PAL) National-scale RCT, 1,100 schools, 182 zones + 4.4m exam scores Gains in taught literacy and basic maths after 2 years; better leaving exams later. Extra teacher PD doubled cost, no extra gain . SD figures UNVERIFIED . https://www.povertyactionlab.org/updates/national-study-zambia-finds-focus-teaching-basics-leads-broad-learning-gains-over-time Joplin plan / cross-grade regrouping Older quasi-experiments Positive (Steenbergen-Hu: g = 0.26). Dated evidence. Developing-country caveat : Kenya and India have very wide within-class dispersion and curricula far above most pupils' level, which makes level-matching more valuable than in a French 6e. Effects on low achievers and peer effects - Correlational and quasi-experimental tracking studies: low tracks often lose (EEF, Lafontaine), largely through curriculum and expectations (Draelants; IGÉSR 2025 observation). - Experimental evidence: low achievers gain (Kenya), or no differential (Steenbergen-Hu 2016). - Peer-group engineering can backfire: Carrell, Sacerdote and West (2013, Econometrica ) placed low-ability US Air Force Academy cadets with high-ability peers and found the low-ability group did worse , because students re-sorted socially ( from memory, UNVERIFIED this session ). Booij, Leuven and Oosterbeek (2017, REStud) found tracking at a Dutch university helped low and middle ability students ( UNVERIFIED ). --- C. Small-group tutoring Nickow, Oreopoulos and Quan (2020), NBER WP 27476 (read from the PDF) 96 RCTs, 732 estimates. Pooled 0.37 SD . Published 2024 version: 0.288 SD (SE 0.029) (https://nssa.stanford.edu/studies/promise-tutoring-prek-12-learning-systematic-review-and-metaanalysis-experimental-evidence). https://www.nber.org/papers/w27476 Moderator (Table 3A) Effect (SD) Studies --- --- --- Teacher tutors 0.50 18 Paraprofessional tutors 0.40 46 Volunteers 0.21 24 Parents 0.23 11 During school 0.40 78 After school 0.21 17 1:1 0.38 67 1:2 0.29 14 1:3 or more 0.36 24 1-2 days/week 0.24 19 3 days/week 0.34 33 4-5 days/week 0.41 46 Grades 6-11 0.16 8 - Authors: ratios above 1:1 "statistically similar" for teachers/paraprofessionals; "little evidence of once-weekly tutoring sessions generating large effect sizes". - Relevant for collège : only 7% of interventions involve grade 6+; secondary effect much smaller (0.16) and thin. Other tutoring evidence Source Result URL --- --- --- Guryan et al. (2023) , AER 113(3), 738-765, Saga/Chicago, 9th-10th grade Daily 45-50 min, 2:1 , paid tutors, inside the timetable. Math scores +0.18 to 0.40 SD (TOT); ITT 0.12 test / 0.22 GPA. Cost $3,500-4,300 /pupil/year. https://voices.uchicago.edu/jensludwig/files/2023/03/Not-too-late-AER-2023.pdf ; https://overdeck.org/research-repository/tutoring/not-too-late-improving-academic-outcomes-among-adolescents/ EEF small-group tuition +4 months , low cost, moderate evidence; primary +6, secondary +4 (QRF version). https://evidenceforlearning.org.au/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/small-group-tuition EEF one-to-one tuition +5 months , moderate evidence (downgraded: many studies not independent). https://evidenceforlearning.org.au/toolkit/one-to-one-tuition National Tutoring Programme , NFER Year 2 (pub. 19 Oct 2023) School-led tutoring: maths KS2/KS4 ≈ +1 month ; English < 1 month . Tuition Partners and Academic Mentors: no gain , small negative associations. More hours → better. < half of tutored pupils disadvantaged. https://nfer.ac.uk/publications/independent-evaluation-of-the-national-tutoring-programme-year-2-impact-evaluation NTP, NFER Year 3 (pub. 27 Sep 2024) KS2 gains ≤ 1 month , maths persists a year; KS4 < 1 month, not sustained. Optimum "above 20 hours per pupil". Group size: NTP guidance capped groups at 1:3 (UNVERIFIED this session). https://www.nfer.ac.uk/publications/national-tutoring-programme-year-3-impact-evaluation/ France, APFEE "Coup de pouce" (Goux, Gurgand, Maurin), RCT 2010-13 ~5,100 CP pupils, 109 schools (Créteil, Lille, Versailles); groups of 5 , 4 × 1.5 h/week, after school . No gain in reading or maths ; more enjoyment of reading, lasting 2 years. https://www.povertyactionlab.org/fr/evaluation/accompagnement-intensif-pour-favoriser-legalite-des-chances-lecole-en-france-apfee Devoirs faits (collège, since 2017) No impact evaluation : a parliamentary answer says a scientific evaluation was "pas envisageable" for a national rollout; DGESCO survey only. https://www.assemblee-nationale.fr/dyn/15/questions/QANR5L15QE6804.pdf (via search summary) Lesson from France and England : scaled, after-school or externally sourced tutoring loses most of the RCT effect. The French APFEE null is after-school, groups of 5. --- D. Conditions under which grouping or tutoring works Condition Evidence Teacher time / timetable? --- --- --- --- 1 Flexible, short-cycle regrouping with frequent reassessment , around a precise skill, not a fixed "niveau" Cnesco 2017 ("flexible et réévalué", limited to one sequence); within-class g 0.19-0.30 vs between-class ≈ 0 (Steenbergen-Hu 2016); IGÉSR 2025: "quasi-absence de mobilité" in failed rollout Yes: assessment and regrouping need common planning slots 2 Same curriculum and high expectations in low groups Between-class grouping "without changing the curriculum" ≈ 0; harm channel is lowered goals (Draelants 2023; IGÉSR 2025: lowered expectations, cut content) Partly: needs shared progressions across teachers 3 Grouping bundled with extra time, not substituting for class time Double-dose algebra +0.15 SD ACT, +8.6 pp college (Cortes et al. 2015); TaRL Haryana dedicated hour +0.15 SD Yes: extra hours = ORS / HSE 4 Teach at the pupil's actual level for part of the day only TaRL (+0.15 to +0.70 SD); Kenya tracking +0.14 SD Timetable 5 Tutoring during the school day, inside the timetable During 0.40 vs after 0.21 SD (Nickow 2020); Saga embedded in schedule; APFEE after-school null Yes: requires timetable slots 6 Small groups: 1:1 to 1:3 (≤ 4); 5+ is no longer tutoring 1:1 0.38, 1:2 0.29, 1:3+ 0.36 (Nickow); Saga 2:1; APFEE groups of 5 null Staffing ratio 7 Dosage ≥ 3 sessions/week, ≥ 20 h per pupil 3 days 0.34, 4-5 days 0.41, 1-2 days 0.24 (Nickow); NTP optimum 20 h (NFER 2024) Yes: hours 8 Trained, paid tutors (teachers or paraprofessionals), not volunteers Teacher 0.50, paraprofessional 0.40, volunteer 0.21 (Nickow); NTP school-led beat external partners Yes: who delivers, under which status 9 Aligned timetables across classes ("heures en barrettes") so groups can be formed across classes Cnesco 2017 recommendation; IGÉSR 2025: uniform full-timetable model creates organisational strain Yes: timetabling 10 Fidelity and school buy-in over scale Best Practice in Setting: half the schools dropped out, null; NTP drive "for scale over quality" (Lampl); Zambia: extra PD added cost, no gain Yes: leadership time, autonomy for heads (IGÉSR rec.) ORS relevance : conditions 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9 depend directly on teacher service time (common planning hours, extra hours, timetable alignment). Under the current French ORS (18 h of teaching for certifiés, no dedicated planning time; figures not re-sourced here, UNVERIFIED), flexible grouping and in-school tutoring require either recognised concertation hours or annualised service. --- 10-line summary 1. The 2024 arrêté (15 Mar 2024) imposed groupes de besoins in 6e-5e français-maths; the CE annulled it on competence only (28 Nov 2024) and said it did not breach the collège unique. 2. A décret + arrêté of 4 Apr 2025 restored it in 6e-5e (4e-3e dropped); the CE upheld them on 27 Feb 2026, again with no ruling on evidence. 3. The arrêté of 10 Mar 2026 made groups optional from rentrée 2026 ("accompagnement pédagogique renforcé"). 4. IGÉSR (May 2025, 39 collèges, not causal): fixed level groups, near-zero mobility, lowered expectations, no benefit for the weakest. No DEPP impact evaluation found. 5. Unions did cite research (Cnesco 2017, Lafontaine, Dupriez-Draelants), but the same Cnesco work endorses temporary homogeneous groups under conditions. 6. The user's claim holds: there is no solid RCT showing grouping is harmful; but there is no solid rich-country RCT showing between-class setting works either (EEF/UCL trial null, poor fidelity). 7. Meta-analyses: between-class grouping ≈ 0 (g 0.04-0.06), within-class 0.19-0.30, cross-grade 0.26; EEF −1 or 0 months for setting, +3 for within-class. 8. The only big clean tracking RCT (Kenya, 2011) found +0.14 SD for all levels; TaRL in India +0.15 to +0.70 SD. 9. Tutoring is the strongest lever (0.37 SD, 96 RCTs), but weaker in secondary (0.16 SD) and in scaled programmes (NTP ≤ 1 month; French APFEE null). 10. It works when flexible, high-expectation, in-school, 1:1 to 1:3, ≥ 3 sessions/week, with aligned timetables and planning time: mostly a teacher-time and timetabling question.

titre: 03 — Teacher inspection and school evaluation: France vs benchmarks
texte: Research brief for the note "organisation de l'école". Compiled 2026-10-26. Convention: every figure has a source, year and URL. UNVERIFIED = from memory or a secondary source I could not check against the primary text this session. Note on sourcing: education.gouv.fr, ccomptes.fr and several OECD/IZA pages blocked automated access (HTTP 403 / Cloudflare), and the web-search budget ran out partway through. Several French facts therefore rest on academy circulars, union documents and press reports of primary texts. Verify them before publication. --- A. France: how teachers are inspected today A1. The PPCR "rendez-vous de carrière" (since 2017-18) Legal basis: décret n° 2017-786 du 5 mai 2017 and arrêté du 5 mai 2017 (cited in the 2022 ministry guide and the Paris 2025-26 circular: https://paris.snes.edu/IMG/pdf/i-dpe-25-00063 circulaire rendez-vous de carriere 2025-2026.pdf ; https://education.gouv.fr/media/48144/download). Before PPCR, each teacher had a numerical "note pédagogique" set at inspections whose timing was irregular. RDV When (classe normale) What it decides Source --- --- --- --- RDV 1 2nd year of the 6th échelon (12 to 24 months of seniority in it) 1-year acceleration to the 7th échelon for 30% of the eligible group Paris circular 2025-26; Martinique PPCR presentation 2017 https://site.ac-martinique.fr/wp-content/uploads/sites/9/2017/04/PPCR-Pr%c3%a9sentation-pour-enseignants.pdf RDV 2 18 to 30 months of seniority in the 8th échelon 1-year acceleration to the 9th échelon for 30% same RDV 3 2nd year of the 9th échelon Timing of promotion to the hors-classe same - Format: a classroom inspection plus two interviews, one with the inspector and one with the chef d'établissement (secondary), no more than 6 weeks apart; teachers are told at least one month (some circulars say 15 days) in advance (SNES Mayotte https://www.mayotte.snes.edu/IMG/pdf/reunion ppcr sur rv carriere.pdf ; Besançon note de service https://ash.circo25.ac-besancon.fr/wp-content/uploads/sites/23/2022/10/Note-de-service-n°2-PPCR-2024.2025.pdf). - Outcome: four-level "appréciation finale" (Excellent / Très satisfaisant / Satisfaisant / À consolider), set by the recteur (or IA-DASEN for primary). - The RDV 3 appréciation is kept for all later hors-classe campaigns ("pérenne"): La Réunion note de service 2023 (https://www.ac-reunion.fr/media/46418/download) uses the RDV 3 appraisal, or the one given in previous hors-classe campaigns. - Outside the RDV, PPCR provides for "accompagnement" (individual or collective, visits, meetings) but with no set frequency (Martinique 2017; Nancy-Metz https://sites.ac-nancy-metz.fr/dsden54-circo/ientoul/sites/ientoul/IMG/pdf/ppcr.pdf). A2. Grid timing: when does the last compulsory inspection happen? Classe normale, certified teachers (CGT grid 2024, https://www.fnte.cgt.fr/sites/default/files/2023-12/Triptyque%20Cat%20A%20Professeur%20Certifi%C3%A9%202024.pdf): échelon durations 1, 1, 2, 2, 2.5, 3, 3, 3.5, 4, 4 years; 11th échelon reached after 26 years at the standard pace (24 with both accelerations). - Cumulative time to reach the 9th échelon at standard pace = 1+1+2+2+2.5+3+3+3.5 = 18 years (my calculation from the grid); RDV 3 falls in year 19 to 20 of service, or 1 to 2 years earlier with accelerations. - Age: with entry around 25 to 27 (after a master's degree and the concours), RDV 3 falls at roughly 43 to 47 years old . This is my estimate, not an official figure, and reclassement on entry (prior service) moves it earlier. The note's claim of "~40-45" is in the right range but slightly young for a standard career. A3. Is "after the 9th échelon, no more inspection" accurate? Broadly yes for compulsory, career-linked inspection. Not literally. After RDV 3 What happens Classroom inspection required? --- --- --- Hors-classe promotion Uses the RDV 3 appréciation, kept until promotion No Classe exceptionnelle (open from the 5th hors-classe échelon, 4th for agrégés) Recteur's appraisal on the I-Prof file, informed by avis of the inspector and of the chef d'établissement (Excellent to À consolider / "très favorable"…); avis cannot be appealed No inspection required by the texts I found; avis can be written from the file (Reims 2024 https://www.reims.snes.edu/IMG/pdf/240325 acces classe exceptionnelle prof agreges.pdf ; Grenoble 2025 https://www.grenoble.snes.edu/IMG/pdf/2025-243 circulaire classe ex et hc.pdf ; Paris https://www.ac-paris.fr/media/58665/download). Whether inspectors visit before an avis: UNVERIFIED , varies by academy "4th RDV" Mentioned in a 2017 Martinique academy presentation as linked to classe exceptionnelle. Not in the national texts as summarised by other circulars Treat as UNVERIFIED / probably inaccurate Ad hoc inspection Possible: "accompagnement", teacher's request, difficulties or complaints, newly arrived teachers Not scheduled Since décret n° 2024-727 du 6 juillet 2024, recteurs (not the minister) draw up the classe exceptionnelle tables for agrégés (Reims 2025 https://www.reims.snes.edu/IMG/pdf/250303 acces classe exceptionnelle prof agreges.pdf). Suggested wording for the note: "Depuis 2017, un enseignant n'a plus d'inspection obligatoire après son troisième rendez-vous de carrière, à la deuxième année du 9e échelon, soit environ 19 ans de carrière. Il peut lui rester plus de 20 ans à enseigner sans aucune visite programmée." A4. Frequency and cost of inspection - Cour des comptes (as quoted by AEF, 9 March 2018, via SGEN-CFDT https://sgen-cfdt.fr/contenu/uploads/2018/03/9-03-18.pdf): 170,000 inspections (year not stated); one inspection = 50 to 60% of a working day, so 85,000 to 102,000 days, or 400 to 490 FTE, 15 to 20% of available IEN and IA-IPR time . Cour: "Il est anormal que non seulement les inspections aient peu de conséquences sur la gestion du corps enseignant, mais également sur les aspects pédagogiques". The source report is probably the Cour's report on teacher evaluation or "Gérer les enseignants autrement" (Oct. 2017): UNVERIFIED which report . - The same AEF note says the Cour stresses that, unlike many countries, French teacher evaluation does not use pupils' progress and rarely uses parents' or pupils' views. - Historical frequency before PPCR: commonly cited as once every 6 to 7 years in secondary, with wide variation (some teachers not inspected for over 10 years). UNVERIFIED : I could not reach a primary source this session. The SNES Lille 2017 slides note the "fréquence aléatoire des inspections" before the reform (https://lille.snes.edu/IMG/pdf/diaporama comparatif nouvelle evaluation outil lutte pedagogique jfc mars2017.pdf). A5. Inspector numbers and workload Indicator Figure Source --- --- --- Territorial inspectors (IEN + IA-IPR) ~3,650 (Cour des comptes 2022); 3,799 at 31 Dec 2021 (ministry) Sénat QE n° 00499, answer 8 Dec 2022 https://www.senat.fr/questions/base/2022/qSEQ220700499.html New posts +100 IA-IPR (3-year plan, 2020-2022); +80 at rentrée 2022 (60 primary, 20 secondary), largely for home-schooling and hors-contrat checks same Teachers per inspector, primary public, 2020 229 national ; 307 in Seine-Saint-Denis Cour des comptes référé, reported by Acteurs publics, May 2022 https://acteurspublics.fr/articles/la-cour-des-comptes-preconise-de-recentrer-les-missions-des-inspecteurs-de-leducation/ Teachers per inspector, secondary public, 2020 137 (Limoges) to 228 (Versailles) same Share of inspector activity on individual teacher evaluation ~30% (primary), 20 to 30% (secondary) same IA-IPR recruitment 2023 78 of 80 posts filled concours report 2023 (via search summary; ministry page blocked) Split IEN vs IA-IPR: not found this session. Order of magnitude often cited: ~1,600 IA-IPR and ~2,100 IEN ( UNVERIFIED ). At ~229 teachers per primary inspector, one inspection per teacher per year would mean ~229 inspections per inspector a year, roughly one per working day. Every two years: ~115 a year. At 50 to 60% of a day each (Cour figure), that is 57 to 69 days, about 30 to 35% of a ~200-day year . Today individual evaluation already takes ~30% of activity, so a 1-to-2-year cycle needs either more inspectors, shorter visits, or delegation (peers, chefs d'établissement). This is my arithmetic: state it as an order of magnitude only. A6. Missions: the "morcellement" - Cour des comptes, référé "Les inspecteurs territoriaux des 1er et 2nd degrés de l'Éducation nationale" (sent Jan. 2022, published 3 May 2022): "L'activité des inspecteurs est de plus en plus morcelée et cet éparpillement s'effectue au détriment de leur mission première, qui reste le suivi des enseignants et l'appui pédagogique" (quoted by SNCI-FO https://fo-fnecfp.fr/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/22-05-05-Refere-de-la-cour-des-comptes.pdf). Teacher monitoring has become the "variable d'ajustement" of their activity. - Missions listed: teacher evaluation, organising exams and concours, promoting national reforms, checking home schooling (instruction en famille), administrative and pedagogical steering of primary schools with directors and municipalities (Acteurs publics, above). - Individual evaluation leaves little room for team meetings, advisory visits and support for new teachers. - 6 recommendations, including: "revue sélective des missions" to refocus on pedagogical support for teachers and teams; a target headcount per academy; functional rapprochement of primary and secondary inspection corps. - Ministry answer (Dec 2022): a review of inspector missions "à partir de 2023" (Sénat QE above). Outcome not found . - IGEN-IGAENR, "Rôle et positionnement des inspecteurs du second degré en académie" (Oct. 2016, after the circular of 11 Dec 2015 on inspectors' missions): the job of IA-IPR / IEN ET-EG / IEN IO has gained academic steering and support to établissements on top of inspection, and needs to be "mieux équilibré et régulé" (https://www.education.gouv.fr/igesr/role-et-positionnement-des-inspecteurs-du-second-degre-en-academie-463599, page blocked; content from search summary and Acteurs publics "les inspecteurs ont la pression" https://acteurspublics.fr/articles/a-leducation-nationale-les-inspecteurs-ont-la-pression/). - Référents laïcité, EAC, numérique : I found no official document listing these as inspector missions. In practice many academies name IA-IPR or IEN as référents (laïcité et fait religieux, EAC, numérique, égalité filles-garçons, harcèlement…). Keep this claim illustrative and UNVERIFIED unless an academy organigram is cited. A7. Teachers' views (TALIS 2024, lower secondary) OECD, Results from TALIS 2024 – Country note: France (Oct. 2025) https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2025/10/results-from-talis-2024-country-notes eafd703e/france 714d7439/50507701-en.pdf Indicator France OECD avg --- --- --- Principal "provides useful feedback to teachers and staff" 71% 77% Novice teachers (≤5 yrs) with an assigned mentor 17% 26% Recent arrivals who took part in induction (formal or informal) 56% (+36 pts since 2018) 72% Teachers who can rely on each other 81% (−4 pts since 2018) 86% Teachers with high curriculum autonomy appraised less than once a year or never 61% n.a. in note - TALIS 2018, primary (DEPP note): among its European neighbours, France is where support after a teacher's appraisal is least frequent , whatever the method (https://education.gouv.fr/media/72610/download, via search summary). The TALIS 2018 share of French teachers "never" receiving feedback: not found ; do not quote a number. --- B. School (établissement) evaluation in France: the CEE - Legal basis : loi n° 2019-791 du 26 juillet 2019 "pour une école de la confiance" created the Conseil d'évaluation de l'école (CEE), which sets the method and tools for self-evaluation and external evaluation of schools and ensures they happen "selon une périodicité régulière" (CEE framework, via https://www.education.gouv.fr/le-conseil-d-evaluation-de-l-ecole/conseil-d-evaluation-de-l-ecole-l-evaluation-des-ecoles-et-des-etablissements-du-second-degre-340814). The CEE replaced the Cnesco as the official evaluator. Its members include ministry representatives, MPs and qualified persons (Banque des territoires, 14 Mar 2022). - Cycle : recteurs schedule evaluations so that all public and private-under-contract établissements are evaluated every 5 years, ~20% a year (IH2EF https://www.ih2ef.gouv.fr/evaluation-des-etablissements-scolaires). Second-degree framework adopted 8 July 2020, updated 8 June 2023, methodological guide for external evaluation Jan. 2024. Primary-school framework adopted 5 Feb 2026. - Process : (1) self-evaluation by the school community (staff, pupils, parents, partners); (2) external evaluation: "analyse distanciée des indicateurs et des pièces du dossier d'auto-évaluation, une observation des lieux et des pratiques et des échanges" with stakeholders (CEE cahier des charges); (3) report and contract/project. - Who evaluates externally : "cadres mobilisés par les évaluations en académie", trained by IH2EF with the CEE (IH2EF). In practice small teams of inspectors (IA-IPR, IEN) and personnels de direction from other schools, with a deontology charter (https://www.education.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/document/charte-d-ontologie-eval-externe-2d-pdf-518858.pdf). The exact team composition is UNVERIFIED ; I could not open the Jan. 2024 guide. Key point for the note: external evaluators are the same inspectors who inspect teachers, plus peer heads . There is no separate, dedicated corps. - Progress : Campaign Coverage Source --- --- --- 2020-21 (1st) ~950 collèges and lycées, just over 9% Banque des territoires, 14 Mar 2022 https://www.banquedesterritoires.fr/evaluation-des-colleges-et-lycees-les-collectivites-encore-trop-discretes 2021-22 ~735 primary schools evaluated (CEE délibération 2023-01) via search summary of education.gouv.fr to 2023-24 ~80% of secondary établissements; ~34% of primary schools CEE bilan 2023-24 https://www.education.gouv.fr/le-conseil-d-evaluation-de-l-ecole/bilan-national-de-la-campagne-d-evaluation-des-ecoles-et-des-etablissements-2023-2024-470429 to 2024-25 ~90% of secondary établissements since 2020; 54% of primary schools since 2021-22 (19% in 2024-25 alone) CEE bilan 2024-25 https://www.education.gouv.fr/le-conseil-d-evaluation-de-l-ecole/bilan-national-de-la-campagne-d-evaluation-des-ecoles-et-des-etablissements-2024-2025-470426 2025-26 2nd five-year cycle begins IH2EF colloquium, 19-21 May 2025 https://www.ih2ef.gouv.fr/evaluation-des-etablissements-bilan-et-perspectives-20252030-le-colloque-du-cee - Limits : reports are not graded and not systematically published school by school ( UNVERIFIED ; check the CEE). Local authorities were poorly informed and rarely involved (Banque des territoires 2022). Inspector unions call the evaluation "chronophage", saying it pulls IEN away from their circonscriptions (SNCI-FO, May 2022). Evaluation of outcomes for the CEE system: none found . --- C. England: Ofsted and in-school appraisal C1. Framework timeline Date Change Source --- --- --- Sept 2014 Ofsted stops grading individual lessons; inspectors record evidence only Tes Aug 2014 https://www.tes.com/magazine/archive/ofsted-scraps-grades-individual-lessons ; Ofsted note https://dera.ioe.ac.uk/20770/1/Information%20for%20teachers%20about%20inspection%20-%20lesson%20observations.pdf Sept 2019 Education Inspection Framework (EIF): 4 judgements (quality of education, behaviour and attitudes, personal development, leadership) + overall grade 1-4 (Outstanding, Good, Requires improvement, Inadequate) UNVERIFIED this session (well known) Jan 2023 Death of head teacher Ruth Perry after her school was downgraded from Outstanding to Inadequate (safeguarding); inquest Dec 2023 found the inspection contributed to her death Express & Star / ITV, 2024 https://www.itv.com/news/meridian/2023-12-11/we-must-build-on-ruth-perrys-legacy-to-prevent-repeat-tragedy-keegan 2 Sept 2024 Government scraps single-word overall judgements, with immediate effect; Gilbert learning review published 3 Sept 2024 https://www.expressandstar.com/uk-news/one-word-ofsted-judgments-for-schools-scrapped-by-government-5769180 10 Nov 2025 Renewed EIF with report cards ; routine state-school inspections resumed 1 Dec 2025; toolkit v2.0 applies from 7 Sept 2026 https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/education-inspection-framework/education-inspection-framework-for-use-from-november-2025 C2. The 2025 report card (primary source: gov.uk EIF Nov 2025) - Evaluation areas : Inclusion; Curriculum and teaching; Achievement; Attendance and behaviour; Personal development and well-being; Leadership and governance; Early years and Post-16 where relevant; Safeguarding = met / not met . - 5-point scale per area : Urgent improvement / Needs attention / Expected standard / Strong standard / Exceptional. No overall grade. "Needs attention" is presented as an early warning, not a failure (gov.uk "Understanding Ofsted report cards", 1 Dec 2025 https://www.gov.uk/guidance/understanding-ofsted-report-cards-and-grades). - Frequency : routine inspection usually about every 4 years . The statutory requirement is within 5 school years of the end of the year of the last inspection (The Key, 2025-26 https://schoolleaders.thekeysupport.com/school-evaluation-and-improvement/inspection/after-inspection/frequency-inspection-overview/ ; Waltham Forest letter to parents Jan 2026). These are secondary sources, consistent with each other. - Monitoring (Ofsted monitoring operating guide, Nov 2025 https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/school-inspection-toolkit-operating-guide-and-information/school-monitoring-operating-guide-for-inspectors-for-use-from-november-2025): "needs attention" schools get a monitoring inspection no later than 24 months after the report card; schools in a category of concern can get up to 5 on-site monitoring inspections within 18 months . This is risk-based targeting. - Teams : 2 inspectors per day in small schools, 3 on day 1 otherwise (Ofsted blog FAQ, 11 Dec 2025 https://educationinspection.blog.gov.uk/2025/12/11/school-inspections-frequently-asked-questions/). - Inspectors : employed His Majesty's Inspectors (~343 HMI + 88 Senior HMI, FDA union survey May 2025 https://www.fda.org.uk/news/new-research-reveals-98-per-cent-of-his-majestys-inspectors-are-overworked, not an official count) plus contracted Ofsted Inspectors , many of them serving practitioners (heads and senior leaders). Contracting was brought in-house in 2015 to raise the share of teams with a serving leader (Ofsted Annual Report 2014-15). Current share of serving practitioners: not found . - No grading of individual teachers : Ofsted grades the school, not teachers or lessons, since 2014. C3. Teacher appraisal (done by the school, not Ofsted) - Education (School Teachers' Appraisal) (England) Regulations 2012 (SI 2012/115, in force Sept 2012): annual appraisal of every teacher by the head teacher or a delegate, with written objectives, classroom observation and a written report including a pay recommendation (legislation.gov.uk https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2012/115, UNVERIFIED this session; SI 2012/2055 only amended the induction exclusion https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2012/2055). - 2024 : the School Teachers' Pay and Conditions Document 2024 removed the requirement that all pay progression be linked to appraisal , from 1 Sept 2024. Appraisal remains compulsory (school policy quoting STPCD 2024 https://www.kingedwin.notts.sch.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Appraisal-Policy-for-Teachers.pdf). Check the STPCD text before quoting. - Takeaway : England separates school inspection (external, Ofsted, every ~4 years) from teacher appraisal (internal, annual, by line managers). C4. Evidence on Ofsted effects Study Design Result --- --- --- Hussain (2015), J. Human Resources 50(1): 189-221 (not J. Public Econ.) https://jhr.uwpress.org/content/50/1/189 Fail vs non-fail, DiD/IV, primary schools Fail rating raises test scores; largest gains for low prior attainers; no evidence of gaming ; no effect for schools rated highly. Effect ~0.12 SD per a RISE survey table https://riseprogramme.org/node/355.html (secondary) Allen & Burgess (2012), CMPO WP 12/287 https://ideas.repec.org/p/bri/cmpowp/12-287.html Fuzzy RD, schools just failing vs just passing, a decade of data Just-failed schools improve by ~10% of a pupil SD over 2 to 3 years, including in core subjects; little effect for low-ability pupils. Working paper; published version not found Recent work on fail judgements and post-2024 reforms n.a. Not found this session --- D. Other benchmarks and causal evidence on teacher evaluation D1. Systems (all UNVERIFIED this session; primary pages unreachable) System Teacher evaluation School evaluation --- --- --- Ontario Teacher Performance Appraisal (Education Act Part X.2, O. Reg. 99/02): new teachers appraised twice in the first 12 months; experienced teachers once every 5-year cycle by the principal, with an Annual Learning Plan each year; rating Satisfactory / Unsatisfactory School and board improvement plans; no inspectorate Netherlands Teachers not evaluated by the Inspectorate; done by school boards Inspectie van het Onderwijs: since 2017, board-level inspection roughly every 4 years plus risk-based school investigations; schools can be rated "zeer zwak" (very weak) or "onvoldoende" (inadequate), with publication Germany (Länder) Schulaufsicht (Schulrat / Schulamt) does periodic "dienstliche Beurteilung" of civil-servant teachers, e.g. Bavaria every 4 years; Fachberater give subject advice separately from appraisal Several Länder ran school inspections from the 2000s and later scaled them back or turned them into internal-evaluation support Singapore Enhanced Performance Management System (EPMS): annual appraisal by the reporting officer (HoD / vice-principal) against competencies, with work review, linked to bonus and promotion; a separate track for teachers moving to senior/lead/master teacher roles School Excellence Model, self-assessment with external validation D2. Causal evidence that evaluation itself improves teaching Study Setting Design Effect --- --- --- --- Taylor & Tyler (2012), AER 102(7): 3628-51 https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.102.7.3628 Cincinnati TES, mid-career teachers Within-teacher, before/after a scheduled evaluation year; observed 4 times in the year (3 by external peer evaluators , high-performing experienced teachers; 1 by the principal); evaluated year 1, year 4, then every 5 years Students of a teacher after TES score ~10% of a SD higher in math than the same teacher's students before; gains persist and are largest for initially weak teachers (NBER WP 16877 text) Steinberg & Sartain (2015), Education Finance and Policy 10(4): 535-72 https://ideas.repec.org/a/tpr/edfpol/v10y2015i4p535-572.html Chicago Excellence in Teaching Project, principal-teacher observation and dialogue (Danielson framework) Randomised staggered rollout, 44 vs 48 elementary schools (2008-09 / 2009-10) Cohort 1 outperformed in reading after year 1 (math not significant); gains concentrated in higher-achieving, lower-poverty schools. Magnitude ~0.10 SD reading: UNVERIFIED Burgess, Rawal & Taylor (2021), J. Labor Econ. 39(4): 1155-86 https://ideas.repec.org/a/ucp/jlabec/doi10.1086-712997.html 82 English secondary schools, teachers observe and score each other (EEF-funded) School-level RCT; teachers randomly assigned to observer/observee +0.07 SD in GCSE maths and English; both roles benefit, observers possibly more; doubling observations did not raise effects ; larger for low-performing teachers Reading for the note: the gains come from structured observation with a rubric and feedback , even when stakes are low (Burgess et al.) and even when done by peers (Cincinnati, England). Frequency matters less than quality: doubling observations added nothing in England, and Cincinnati's effects come from one intensive year every 5 years. --- Summary: the most useful comparisons for a French note 1. Since PPCR (2017), French teachers have 3 compulsory inspections, at the 6th, 8th and 9th échelons; the last falls around year 19 of a career (~43-47 years old, my estimate), leaving 20+ years without a scheduled visit. The claim is accurate in substance; say "après le 3e rendez-vous de carrière (9e échelon)". 2. After that, hors-classe uses the kept RDV 3 appraisal and classe exceptionnelle uses file-based avis from the inspector and the head: no compulsory classroom visit. 3. Capacity is the binding constraint: ~3,800 inspectors (2021), 229 primary teachers per inspector (2020), and individual evaluation already takes 20-30% of their time. A 1-to-2-year cycle needs about 30-35% of inspector time (my arithmetic) or delegation. 4. The Cour des comptes (May 2022) already diagnosed "morcellement" and asked for a "revue sélective des missions" to refocus on pedagogical support. Use it as the authority for refocusing. 5. TALIS 2024: French teachers get less useful feedback from principals than the OECD average (71% vs 77%), and fewer novices have a mentor (17% vs 26%). 6. School evaluation exists (CEE, 2019 law, every 5 years, ~90% of secondary schools covered by 2024-25), but it is run by the same inspectors and heads. A separate specialised body would be new; the closest models are Ofsted and the Dutch Inspectie. 7. England separates the two jobs: Ofsted inspects schools (~every 4 years, 5-point report card by area since Nov 2025, no teacher grading since 2014); heads appraise every teacher annually (2012 regulations). 8. Ofsted's risk-based targeting (monitoring within 24 months for "needs attention", up to 5 visits in 18 months for schools of concern) suits a French school-evaluation body better than a uniform cycle. 9. Causal evidence: being failed by Ofsted raises scores ~0.1 SD (Allen & Burgess 2012; Hussain 2015). Structured teacher evaluation raises student scores 0.07-0.10 SD (Taylor & Tyler 2012; Burgess et al. 2021). 10. Design lesson: what works is rubric-based observation with feedback, often by trained peers; extra frequency adds little (doubling observations: no gain). A "every 1-2 years" pledge is more credible as frequent formative visits (peers, heads, conseillers pédagogiques) plus a rarer inspector evaluation, than as a full inspection every year.

titre: 04. Inclusion of pupils with disabilities: Italy, New York City, Québec
texte: Research note for note-organisation-ecole , 26 October 2026. Adds to note-penser-pratique/handicap-review.md (France facts, Italy row I1-I3, evidence E1-E7), which is not repeated here. "Primary" = figure read in the source document itself. "Secondary" = read in a press or third-party summary. UNVERIFIED = not confirmed in any source read. The web-search budget ran out before the Québec CDPDJ 2018 study itself could be read; its findings below come from the CDPDJ's own 2023 synthesis. A. Italy: which "2018 study"? Candidates Candidate Year What it found Status --- --- --- --- ISTAT, L'inclusione scolastica: accessibilità, qualità dell'offerta e caratteristiche degli alunni con sostegno , a.s. 2017-18 English release 21 Dec 2018; Italian 3 Jan 2019 First edition extended to nursery and upper secondary. 272 167 pupils with support (3.1 % of pupils), 156 000 support teachers, 48 000 assistenti all'autonomia e comunicazione . 14 h a week of support on average. Only 32 % of schools accessible for motor disability. 36 % of support teachers drawn from ordinary (non-specialised) lists. Primary for the counts (EN PDF); 36 % and 1.5 pupils per teacher secondary. IT PDF, EN PDF ISTAT, L'inclusione scolastica degli alunni con disabilità , a.s. 2018-19 6 Feb 2020 284 000 pupils with disabilities (3.3 %). ~173 000 support teachers, 1.6 pupils per support teacher against a legal ratio of 2 (L. 244/2007). 36 % of support teachers from ordinary lists (47 % North, 21 % South). 57.6 % of primary/lower-secondary pupils changed support teacher from the year before (61 % North); 10 % changed during the year. 14.1 h of support a week (15.4 primary, 12.3 lower secondary), +18 % in five years. ~6 % of families appealed to the administrative court (TAR) over hours (10.2 % South). 54 000 assistants (4.8 pupils per assistant; 14 in Campania). Pupils with limited autonomy spend 2.6 h a week outside class, 6.4 h for the most severe, 8.2 h in the North. 66 % miss overnight trips. Primary (PDF read). PDF Fondazione Agnelli, Treellle, Caritas, Gli alunni con disabilità nella scuola italiana: bilancio e proposte 2011 , not 2018 Judged 30 years of integration largely a failure: over-medicalised certification by local health authorities, "delegation" of the disabled pupil to the support teacher. Proposed moving most support teachers to ordinary posts and keeping 10-20 000 specialists in Centri Risorse per l'Integrazione . Secondary. Caritas PDF; summary Ianes, L'evoluzione dell'insegnante di sostegno (Erickson) 2014 Turn 80 % of support teachers into co-teaching curricular teachers, 20 % into itinerant expert supervisors; a Trentino pilot followed. Secondary. disabili.com, 17 Apr 2014 D.lgs. 66/2017 (reform) + D.lgs. 96/2019 + DM 182/2020 2017-2020 Replaces the medical diagnosi funzionale with an ICF-based Profilo di funzionamento (from 1 Jan 2019); national PEI models; class-level working group (GLO) sets support hours. DM 182/2020 annulled by a court, later reinstated. Secondary. Lattes summary; OrizzonteScuola European Agency (EASIE) country data; academic outcome evaluations (D'Alessio, Ianes) various Not reached. No causal evaluation of Italian pupils' learning outcomes under inclusion was found. UNVERIFIED Verdict - Most likely candidate: the ISTAT survey released December 2018 / January 2019 (a.s. 2017-18). It is the only "2018" document, and its headline (one support teacher in three untrained) is the one press coverage repeats. Confidence: moderate, about 50 %. If the user remembers the continuity figures (more than half of pupils changing teacher every year), the 2018-19 edition (published Feb 2020) is the better match, and it is the one read in full here. The 2011 Agnelli-Treellle-Caritas report is the main critical study and is often misdated. - What all of them show, beyond the existing I2 row: Italy's problem is not staff numbers (1.6 pupils per support teacher, better than the legal norm) but training and stability : a third untrained, more than half changing teacher each year, and support often delivered outside the class (the "delega" problem). No source shows learning outcomes. B. New York City Structure (NYC Public Schools) Item Figure Source --- --- --- Pupils with an IEP (individualised education programme), 2023-24 188 791 of 813 880 = 23.2 % DOE data at City Council hearing, 30 Jan 2025 (secondary transcript). citymeetings.nyc Service gaps, 2023-24 92 % received all mandated programmes, 95 % all related services; 23 906 (12.9 %) missing at least one service, 1 774 (1 %) none same; the two figures do not reconcile cleanly Continuum general class + supports; ICT (Integrated Co-Teaching: one general + one special-education teacher); SETSS (resource teacher, direct or consultative); special classes (IEP pupils only, e.g. 12:1, 12:1:1 = 12 pupils, 1 teacher, 1 para); District 75 (citywide district of specialised schools/sites for significant needs) DOE overview at the same hearing. citymeetings.nyc; D75 ICT scale and rule ~100 000 pupils in ICT, nearly half of all pupils with disabilities ; pupils with disabilities "must not exceed 40 %" of an ICT class Chalkbeat, 12 Aug 2020. link. State cap of 12 IEP pupils per ICT class (8 NYCRR 200.6(g)): UNVERIFIED Self-contained use 57 000 pupils with disabilities spend 40 % of the day in self-contained classes (2017-18) IncludeNYC testimony (secondary). link Placement is sticky of ~48 000 K-5 IEP pupils, most recommended ICT or self-contained in 2014-15 had the same recommendation two years later; exits from self-contained rare, mostly at school change; ICT availability in the school raises the chance of an ICT placement IBO, Apr 2024 (secondary; IBO site moved). IBO ASD Nest and Horizon (autism programmes in ordinary district schools) - Nest (launched 2003, NYU + DOE): an ICT class inside a mainstream school, two teachers (one general, one special education), no paraprofessional . Kindergarten 12 pupils, 4 autistic ; grades 1-3 16, 4 autistic ; grades 4-5 20, up to 5 autistic (Autism Spectrum News; InsideSchools gives 4:16 for grades 4-5). Plus NYU's Social Development Intervention (SDI) taught in small groups by related-service staff, and specialised teacher training. NYU Nest; Autism Spectrum News - Horizon : special class, 8:1:1 (8 autistic pupils, 1 special-education teacher, 1 para), ABA-informed, inside district schools. MOPD - Scale: Nest in 59 schools with 1 700 pupils (2021-22, secondary) and "more than 90 schools" (NYU, current). All specialised autism programmes: ~5 100 pupils projected, +16 classes / 116 seats for 2025-26 (DOE, Council finance hearing 20 May 2025). A 97 % four-year graduation rate for Nest and Horizon was asserted by a council member: UNVERIFIED. citymeetings.nyc - Evaluation: none causal. The Research Alliance for NYC Schools did a qualitative study (29 staff, 3 schools chosen for fidelity) and is running Taking Flight , a 3-year survey of Nest graduates (2025-2027) benchmarked on the US NLTS-2; no results yet. qualitative; Taking Flight - Selection caveat: Nest admits autistic pupils judged able to follow the general curriculum (cognitive and behavioural criteria), so raw outcomes are not comparable with other settings. 2012 reform: A Shared Path to Success - Pilot 2010, citywide September 2012 . Principle: zoned schools must serve pupils with IEPs (more access to general curriculum), with funding following the pupil and flexible IEPs. Prompted partly by a 2012 Public Advocate report on low inclusion and graduation (secondary). Hubert 2013; Chalkbeat 2013 - Implementation: teachers' union complaints of missing aides and ICT classes where most pupils had disabilities, teachers "overwhelmed" (EdWeek, Oct 2014). - Evaluation: Stiefel, Gottfried, Shiferaw and Schwartz, Is Special Education Improving? Case Evidence from New York City (2005-2015 data): inclusion rose in elementary and middle school, fell in high school ; graduation of pupils with disabilities rose but stayed at ~50 % vs ~80 % for others (figures secondary); descriptive, not causal. NYU Wagner. The Research Alliance did not evaluate the reform itself; its 2019 brief finds autism, emotional disturbance and intellectual disability mostly placed in self-contained classes. brief - State finding, 2019: the NY State Education Department's Compliance Assurance Plan said the city had violated federal law (IDEA) for 13 years and past reforms had "not resulted in the systemic change necessary" (secondary). Chalkbeat, 9 Jul 2019 Persistent problems: litigation Indicator Figure Source --- --- --- Due-process complaints filed 14 000 (2020-21) → 21 000 (2022-23) NYC press release, Jan 2024 (city's own claim). a860-gpp Backlog / delay 11 000 cases unassigned, 282 days average (before 2022) → 119 days (2022-23) after transfer to OATH; legal limit 75 days same; Chalkbeat 2020 Filing rate NY State 517 filings per 10 000 pupils , highest in the US, mostly NYC Manhattan Institute (Weber), Feb 2026. link Carter cases (private tuition reimbursed when the DOE cannot provide FAPE) $47 m (2005) → $1.3 bn (FY2025), 3.25 % of the DOE budget ; $101 000 per pupil same; Chalkbeat, May 2026, finds a large racial gap in who obtains reimbursement. link C. Québec Framework - Politique de l'adaptation scolaire (1999) : ordinary class, near home, is the first option when it helps learning and social integration; otherwise special class or school. The plan d'intervention is mandatory, drawn up by the principal with parents, staff and pupil (Loi sur l'instruction publique, art. 96.14). A pupil is counted as EHDAA/HDAA when a plan d'intervention is declared at 30 September: the count is administrative, not a prevalence (secondary). CISSS Lanaudière - Two categories, two funding logics. Élèves handicapés (codes 14 to 99: autism, language disorder, intellectual disability, etc.) need a professional evaluation matching the diagnosis to obtain a code, which triggers extra funding. Élèves en difficulté (EDAA) need no diagnosis and are funded through general allocations (secondary, FCPQ 2021). The CDPDJ and Protecteur du citoyen both reject this diagnosis-based funding and ask for a needs-based model and a funded minimum threshold of services ; the ministry was piloting a revision in 2023 (CDPDJ 2023 synthesis, primary). - Classes langage (for déficience langagière ) and TSA classes exist as special classes at school-board level; no provincial ratio was found (UNVERIFIED). Facts (OPHQ, Portrait annuel, édition 2025 , published 21 Jan 2026, primary) PDF Indicator (2023-24 unless stated) Figure --- --- HDAA pupils 276 431 = 23.9 % of pupils (22.2 % in 2021-22; +11.9 % in two years) of which handicapés / EDAA 5.2 % / 18.7 % of all pupils Share by level 5.6 % pre-school, 21.2 % primary, 31.4 % secondary Autism among handicapés 44.4 % (41.6 % in 2021-22); language disorder 23.2 % Setting, all HDAA (public) 78.2 % ordinary class , 19.1 % special class, 1.6 % special school Ordinary class by level 68.6 % pre-school, 83.4 % primary, 74.1 % secondary Setting, handicapés only 47.0 % ordinary class, 44.3 % special class Diploma after 7 years, cohort 2016-17 (public) HDAA 49.4 % (gap 38.4 points with other pupils, ~88 %); handicapés 34.7 %; plus qualification 13.7 % / 19.4 % Diploma + qualification after 7 years francophone HDAA 61.8 % vs anglophone 74.0 % Long run (CDPDJ 2023) HDAA share 10.8 % (2001-02) → 21.6 % (2021-22); 25 % of HDAA leave secondary with nothing, ~40 % of coded pupils, vs 13.5 % of others Debates and failures - CDPDJ (2018) systemic study (Ducharme and Magloire), 22 recommendations: right to education "still not acquired"; 73 % of CDPDJ education investigations since 1999 concern HDAA pupils (642 files). In 2023 most recommendations were still not implemented. synthesis, 2023; study (not read) - Protecteur du citoyen (June 2022) , L'élève avant tout , on 86 000 EDAA primary pupils: services organised by available resources, not need; up to 8 months' wait for a first evaluation, then up to 8 months for the service , often more than a school year in total; 39 % of parents told by the school to get a private evaluation, 42 % did ; unstable assignments of support staff; ministry has no data on vacant professional posts (as reported in CDPDJ 2023 synthesis). report - Conseil supérieur de l'éducation (Oct 2017) , Pour une école riche de tous ses élèves : from a segregated to an increasingly inclusive system in 50 years, but difficulties are increasingly concentrated in ordinary classes because selective "projets particuliers" and special classes regroup pupils; a "point de bascule" reached (the "école à trois vitesses" argument). summary PDF - 2023-2028 collective agreement (announced 18 Feb 2024): 4 000 classroom aides for 14 000 classes; a new "class composition" mechanism (extra resources "if possible"); TES pay $65 000 → $77 000. Québec.ca. The FAE's 2023 demands were "more homogeneous" class composition and more enseignants-orthopédagogues for early screening. FAE - 2025 cuts: 570 M$ imposed on the network in summer 2025 (partly relaxed); parents' federation reports missing services for pupils with special needs at the rentrée 2025 and parents paying privately for psychology and special education (Noovo; FCPQ). A national count of new "classes spécialisées" in 2024-25: not found (UNVERIFIED). D. Lessons for France Lesson Evidence --- --- --- 1 Stability of the adult matters as much as numbers. Italy has 1.6 pupils per support teacher, yet 57.6 % change teacher each year and 10 % mid-year. France's AESH turnover is the same risk. Tie support staff to a school (not a pupil) for at least 3 years. ISTAT 2018-19; Protecteur 2022 (unstable assignments) 2 Train before you hire. One Italian support teacher in three is untrained (47 % in the North) despite a specialised diploma track. A support role without a required qualification fills with the untrained when demand grows. ISTAT 2017-18, 2018-19 3 Put specialised units inside ordinary schools, with two teachers. NYC's Nest (12-20 pupils, 4-5 autistic, two teachers, social-skills curriculum) and Horizon (8:1:1) are the closest analogues to UEMA/ULIS-TSA; demand keeps rising (+116 seats in 2025-26). But no causal evaluation exists: France should evaluate its own units from the start. NYU; DOE 2025; Research Alliance 4 Co-teaching needs a cap on concentration. NYC caps pupils with disabilities at 40 % of an ICT class; where caps slipped after 2012, teachers were overwhelmed. Consistent with the 15-20 % threshold in the Swiss study already in the review [E2]. Chalkbeat 2020; EdWeek 2014 5 Supply creates placement. In NYC, a pupil is more likely to get ICT if the school has an ICT class; placements rarely change. French notifications should be reviewed against what is available locally, and units placed where the waiting lists are. IBO 2024 6 Diagnosis-gated funding produces waiting lists and a private market. Québec: up to 16 months from need to service, 42 % of parents pay privately; both watchdogs ask for needs-based funding. France's MDPH gate (21 months for an IME place) is the same mechanism. Fund a first level of help (orthophonie, psychologist) without waiting for the notification. Protecteur 2022; CDPDJ 2018/2023 7 Enforceable rights without supply shift money to lawyers. NYC: 21 000 due-process complaints a year and $1.3 bn in private tuition, with racial gaps in who wins. France's rising referrés over AESH hours risk the same drift; invest in supply first. Manhattan Institute 2026; Chalkbeat 2026; ISTAT (6 % TAR appeals) Caveat for all lessons: none of the three systems has a causal evaluation of its inclusion model. Québec's HDAA diploma gap (49.4 % vs ~88 %) and NYC's (~50 % vs ~80 %) describe outcomes, not the effect of settings. Summary - Italy: most likely "2018 study" = ISTAT inclusion survey a.s. 2017-18 (released Dec 2018 / Jan 2019), ~50 % confidence; the 2018-19 edition (Feb 2020) has the sharpest numbers: 1.6 pupils per support teacher, 36 % untrained, 57.6 % change teacher yearly, 6 % of families go to court. The 2011 Agnelli-Treellle-Caritas report is the main critique, often misdated. - NYC: 23.2 % of pupils have an IEP; ~half of them in two-teacher ICT classes; Nest/Horizon autism units (~5 100 pupils) popular but unevaluated; 2012 reform raised inclusion except in high school; litigation exploded (21 000 complaints, $1.3 bn Carter costs). - Québec: 23.9 % HDAA, 78.2 % in ordinary classes; HDAA diploma rate 49.4 % after 7 years; watchdogs blame diagnosis-based funding and waits of up to 16 months.

titre: 05 — Orientation (careers guidance): France, England, Finland, evidence
texte: Research note, 2026-10-26. Every figure carries its source, year and URL. UNVERIFIED = background knowledge or secondary coverage that I could not check against a primary text in this pass. Unless stated otherwise, the France figures cover public schools under the Ministry of Education. --- A. France A1. Where 3e pupils go (campaign 2025, DGESCO Repères pour l'orientation et l'affectation des élèves 2025 , primary source) Source: https://eduscol.education.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/document/reperes-pour-l-orientation-et-l-affectation-des-eleves-campagne-2025-126290.pdf (666,637 pupils in public 3e; 28.4% hold a bourse) 2025, all public 3e 2de GT 2de pro 1re année CAP Total voie pro --- --- --- --- --- Family requests (final phase) 63.8% 25.5% 10.7% 36.2% Final decisions 61.4% 27.6% 11.0% 38.6% Boursiers: final decisions 47.8% — — 52.2% Non-boursiers: final decisions 66.7% — — 33.3% - Class councils push pupils towards voie pro. Decisions to 2de GT run 2.4 points below requests. For boursiers, the gap between first intentions and final decisions is 9.3 points, against 5.5 for non-boursiers. Boursiers "adjust" downward between the two phases: their choice of 2de GT falls 5.4 points, against 3.6 for non-boursiers (Repères 2025, pp. 6–9). - Provisional advice is the main channel. For boursiers, class councils give 58.8% provisional advice to voie pro, against 37.7% for non-boursiers (p. 9). - Gender. Final decisions to 2de GT: girls 68.3%, boys 54.8% (graph 25). - Apprenticeship. 6.8% of 3e pupils made a final choice of apprenticeship in 2025, up 2 points on 2024. The figure is 4.2% for girls (pp. 27–29). - First wishes in voie pro are hard to get. In 2025 only 58.1% of rank-1 wishes in voie pro were satisfied (2de pro 61.3%, CAP 49.9%), against 87.0% in 2de GT. Lycée professionnel places fell by 3,391 in 2025, and the document states that "la capacité d'accueil en lycée professionnel demeure insuffisante pour répondre à la demande" (table 2, p. ~12). - Formal disagreement is rare. 2.5% of 3e decisions matched none of the family's requests (15,954 out of 648,880). Families can appeal within 3 working days, or claim a one-year maintien (keeping the pupil in the same class) under art. D.331-35. In 17.2% of 3e disagreements the family asked for maintien (graphs 34–35, p. 63). Implication for the recteur's point: redoublement exists only as a family right after a disagreement, not as an option the school team offers. - Trend. DEPP NI 23.40 (Sept. 2023): orientation to 2de GT rose from 61% (3e cohort 2010-11) to 69% (2019-20). The choice between GT and pro "reste fortement lié au passé scolaire ainsi qu'à l'origine sociale", and pupils going to voie pro "ont très majoritairement les résultats scolaires les plus faibles au collège". The two figures are not comparable: NI 23.40 counts cohorts and includes the private sector, while Repères counts the public sector only. https://www.education.gouv.fr/depp/l-orientation-en-fin-de-troisieme-reste-marquee-par-de-fortes-disparites-scolaires-et-sociales-452367 - Géographie de l'École 2021 (DEPP), 3e pupils of 2019 one year later: 64% GT, 28% pro as pupils, 5% apprenticeship, 3% repeat (via the DEPP search snippet; the PDF is not checked, so UNVERIFIED ). A2. Affelnet and the weight of grades - Affelnet-Lycée ranks candidates for each wish with a points score. The score has two separate parts: mastery of the socle commun (8 components on 4 levels) and 3e grades, converted to a common scale. Bonuses for address, bourse status and, in Paris, the collège's IPS (indice de position sociale) are added depending on the académie. Sources: ac-Réunion technical note 2025, https://www.ac-reunion.fr/sites/ac reunion/files/2025-04/note-technique-gestion-des-valuations-affelnet-lyc-e-2025-pour-les-coll-ges-43822.pdf ; Grenoble memento 2017 (socle levels 10/25/40/50 points × coefficient 30, old), https://sacoche.sesamath.net/ doc/DNB Affelnet 2017 memento Grenoble extrait.pdf - For voie pro, grades decide. Selective 2de pro specialities are filled on the grade score. Because demand exceeds places (58.1% first-wish satisfaction), a fall in grades in 3e directly costs a pupil the speciality they wanted. The recteur's point is consistent with this mechanism. No national study isolates the effect of the 3e grade drop, so that specific claim stays UNVERIFIED . A3. Social composition of the voie pro - Rentrée 2023, public sector: children of manual workers ( ouvriers ) or inactive parents make up 55.2% of pupils in lycée professional courses (53.3% in bac pro, 64.8% in CAP), against 29.3% in GT. INSEE TEF from MEN-DEPP data: https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/8242339 - Cour des comptes, RPA 2025 (Rapport public annuel 2025): "à notes et vœux équivalents, les décisions des équipes éducatives sont influencées par le contexte social de l'élève"; "le processus d'orientation tend donc plutôt à amplifier le déterminisme social". Secondary report of the chapter: https://www.banquedesterritoires.fr/lorientation-une-politique-sans-boussole A4. Drop-out and re-orientation in the voie pro DEPP NI 26.24 (June 2026) follows 169,700 pupils who entered 2de pro in 2019 after sitting the DNB (diplôme national du brevet): https://www.education.gouv.fr/sites/default/files/document/deppni-2026-24parcours-scolairesokpdf-517766.pdf - 89% were in 1re pro in 2020, so about 11% left, re-oriented or repeated after the first year. 83% reached terminale pro by 2021. 64% obtained the bac by 2023. - By 2021, 16% of those who failed the DNB had left school, against 7% of those who passed without mention. Pupils who failed the DNB re-orient mostly towards CAP. One in five pupils of the whole cohort did not sit the bac in 2022. - Odds of obtaining the bac rise steeply with the DNB score (odds ratio 2.66 for a score of 18–20 vs 10–11). - Apprentices are a separate measure: 42% of CAP-level contracts are broken within the first 18 months (DARES, 2018 entrants), which counts contract breaks, not drop-outs. https://nouvelle-aquitaine.dreets.gouv.fr/sites/nouvelle-aquitaine.dreets.gouv.fr/IMG/pdf/art actualites etude dares 160125.pdf (via search snippet) - No national DEPP figure for drop-out in the 1st year of school-based CAP was found. UNVERIFIED for CAP. A5. Geography and rural youth - INSEE Première n°1888 (Jan. 2022), census 2018. 93.8% of rural 15–17-year-olds attend school outside their commune, and their average distance to the lycée is 23.2 km , double the collège distance (11.3 km). In very sparse rural communes the distance is 1.7 times that in rural communes close to a town. Rural 16–24-year-olds are more often apprentices. https://www.insee.fr/fr/statistiques/6035523 (PDF IP1888). This confirms the recteur's "~20 km" . - DEPP NI 23.19 (2023), indice d'éloignement (remoteness index). The most remote lycées are more often agricultural or small public lycées, more often have a boarding house ( internat ), and "la voie professionnelle y est plus souvent représentée". https://www.education.gouv.fr/depp/une-mesure-de-l-eloignement-des-lycees-452292 (page 403; content via search snippet) - Berlioux report (5 March 2020) , Orientation et égalité des chances dans la France des zones rurales et des petites villes . It concerns about 10 million young people and points to deficits in information, transport and networks. In the IFOP survey for the report, 48% of 17–23-year-olds in small towns had done or planned "ambitious" higher studies, against 67% in the Paris agglomeration. https://www.centre-inffo.fr/?p=349614 (the report PDF returned 404, so figures come from secondary coverage) - Eduscol: rural families "privilégient davantage une orientation de proximité géographique vers la voie professionnelle" (the Territoires éducatifs ruraux programme). https://eduscol.education.gouv.fr/4818/territoires-ruraux-et-de-montagne - Cour des comptes RPA 2025: 85% of rural youth are satisfied with their lycée assignment, "comme ailleurs" (Banque des Territoires, above). Nuance: the problem lies in the choice of courses, not in satisfaction with the assignment. - Défenseure des droits (3 June 2025): régions "plus soucieuses de pousser les élèves vers les emplois disponibles localement que de favoriser leur mobilité géographique" (L'Humanité, 4 June 2025, press summary of the report Le droit à l'orientation dans l'enseignement secondaire : un droit à déployer pour tous les jeunes ). https://eno.ombudsman.europa.eu/home/news/archives-2025/maincontent/orientation-scolaire-un-droit-so.html A6. Resources: hours, PsyEN, CIO, régions, professeurs principaux Item Figure Source --- --- --- Lycée GT orientation time (2018 reform) 54 h/year "à titre indicatif" , 2de to terminale Rectorat Bordeaux 2018 https://ent2d.ac-bordeaux.fr/disciplines/ses/wp-content/uploads/sites/9/2018/10/Fiche Acc orientation 2nde.pdf ; AN QE 20269 (15th leg.) https://www.assemblee-nationale.fr/dyn/15/questions/QANR5L15QE20269.pdf Total resources for orientation ~8,000 FTE, ~€400m/year Cour des comptes RPA 2025 (Banque des Territoires) Dissatisfied with orientation information and advice 35% of collégiens, 25% of lycéens same "Orientation subie" (felt as imposed) 40% of the young people concerned same First wish not obtained 25–30% of pupils same Vocational diplomas 363, "peu lisibles" same Use of regional resources (2022) 22% of collèges and lycées use regional documentation;
